---
title: "Quick commerce puts the bullwhip remedies to work"
date: 2026-10-29
article-id: FDL-2026-001
field: Retail supply chain
categories: [Bullwhip effect, Behavioral operations, Simulation]
keywords: [quick commerce, inventory, replenishment, demand forecasting, Walmart M5]
abstract: >
  Daily replenishment, shorter lead times and shared sales information implement
  the remedies proposed in the classic bullwhip literature. An order-up-to model
  explains how these choices reduce amplification, and a simulation on Walmart
  sales finds an 87% reduction between modeled traditional and quick-commerce
  networks. Fragmentation raises inventory while weakening availability.
  An accounting identity separates temporary opening orders and channel-switch
  destocking from changes in shopper demand.
---

In their 1997 *Sloan Management Review* article, [Lee, Padmanabhan and Whang](https://sloanreview.mit.edu/article/the-bullwhip-effect-in-supply-chains/) described a puzzle at Procter & Gamble. Retail sales of Pampers fluctuated moderately, while distributors’ orders to P&G varied much more. P&G called this the bullwhip effect. The authors identified four causes: demand forecast updating, order batching, price fluctuation, and rationing and shortage gaming. These could arise from rational decisions within the supply chain.

<!-- hero: charts/e08_structure.png. The structural comparison supports the central claim across forecast settings and product segments. The gain chart explains the unconstrained policy; transition peaks are separate inventory-accounting effects. -->

The lineage reaches back to Forrester’s industrial dynamics (1958) and [Sterman’s Beer Game research (1989)](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.35.3.321). Lee and colleagues focused attention on the information and incentives facing independent businesses. Their remedies were concrete: share point-of-sale information, order smaller quantities more often, shorten lead times, and allocate scarce supply using past sales.

Quick commerce puts several of those remedies into practice. Our argument combines a linear ordering model with a simulation driven by recorded sales: faster, coordinated replenishment substantially reduces amplification, while fragmented inventories and channel transitions create different operational problems.

## Why layered chains amplify orders

The classic setting has several stocking tiers, batched orders, long delivery waits and limited shared sales information. It also provides a useful model of India’s traditional trade: orders move from kiranas through wholesalers and distributors toward brands. Goods move in the opposite direction.

Each tier forecasts what its customers will order and holds stock to cover the wait for replenishment. A forecast revision therefore changes both expected sales and the desired inventory position.

The following result describes that mechanism without requiring normally distributed or independent demand. Let reviews occur every $R$ days, delivery take $L$ days, and
$$
a=1-(1-\alpha)^R,\qquad \beta=1-a,\qquad m=\frac{R+L}{R}.
$$
Here $X_t$ is input during review period $t$, $F_t=\beta F_{t-1}+aX_t$ is its forecast, and the target is $S_t=mF_t+s$ with fixed safety allowance $s$.

Forecast revisions amplify demand cycles by different amounts; the observed bullwhip depends on which cycles demand contains.

::: {#thm-filter}
## Amplification filter

Assume $0<a\leq1$, $m>0$, complete accounting for inventory obligations, unrestricted signed orders, and backlogged unmet demand. For the stationary solution,
$$
q_t=X_t+m(F_t-F_{t-1}),\qquad
H(z)=1+ma\frac{1-z}{1-\beta z}.
$$
If $X_t$ is covariance-stationary with finite, positive variance and spectral density $f_X$, its variance ratio is
$$
\mathcal B=
\frac{\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|H(e^{-i\omega})|^2f_X(\omega)\,d\omega}
{\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}f_X(\omega)\,d\omega}.
$$
For stationary seasonal components with spectral lines, replace $f_X(\omega)d\omega$ by the spectral measure.
:::

::: {.proof}
Between reviews, input reduces inventory position by $X_t$. Restoring the position to $S_t$ requires $q_t=X_t+S_t-S_{t-1}$. Exponential smoothing gives $F=a(1-\beta B)^{-1}X$, where $B$ is the review-period lag operator. The stable filter therefore satisfies $f_q=|H|^2f_X$.
:::

By @lem-gain, gain rises toward faster cycles. Long delivery waits increase the inventory adjustment attached to each forecast revision.

When each tier learns from the previous tier’s orders, it processes an already distorted signal.

::: {#prp-tiers}
## Cascaded forecasts and shared demand

Consider tiers on a common, aligned review clock, with common $a$ and protection factors $m_j$. Write $G(z)=(1-z)/(1-\beta z)$. Forecasting from incoming orders gives
$$
H_{\mathrm{cascade}}=\prod_j(1+m_j aG).
$$
If every tier instead forecasts the same shopper-input sequence, while passing on its child’s orders,
$$
H_{\mathrm{shared}}=1+aG\sum_jm_j.
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
Without sharing, $q_j=H_jq_{j-1}$. With sharing, $q_j=q_{j-1}+m_jaGX$. Iterating the first recursion multiplies filters; summing the second adds forecast adjustments.
:::

This multiplication concerns frequency-specific gains, not a product of separately averaged bullwhip ratios. The classical forecasting analyses of Chen and colleagues (2000) establish closely related effects of smoothing, lead times and information.

The simulated traditional chain exhibits the predicted upstream accumulation (@fig-upstream). Its median weekly swing ratio rises from 1.3× at stores to 2.7× at wholesalers and 9.0× at the distributor. Here the swing ratio compares each tier’s weekly order variance with weekly shopper-input variance; it does not compare order volumes.

![**Swings grow at every step up the traditional chain.** Each point is the swing ratio for the median product: the variance of weekly orders placed by that tier, divided by the variance of weekly shopper input. Traditional retail climbs from 1.3× at stores to 9.0× at the national distributor. Quick commerce reaches only 1.2× at the platform hub. Shading shows the middle half of products.](charts/e01_upstream.png){#fig-upstream fig-alt="Orders become much more variable upstream in the traditional simulation than in quick commerce."}

## Faster replenishment implements the remedies

A coordinated dark-store-and-hub network can replenish daily, share sales records and shorten delivery waits. In our model, daily reviews remove weekly batching, and coordinated ordering excludes independent buyers inflating allocation requests. Shorter protection horizons reduce forecast-update amplification; they do not eliminate it. Platforms can also run discounts, whose effects are outside this paper’s scope.

The same shopper input produces a swing ratio of 1.2× in the quick-commerce structure against 9.0× in traditional retail, approximately 87% lower. Daily reviews deliver the largest reduction along the structural comparison: after pooling the middle tier, the ratio falls from 9.5× to 1.8× (@fig-structure).

![**Daily ordering does most of the work.** Each row changes one thing from the row above, moving step by step from the traditional chain (top) to quick commerce (bottom). Switching from weekly to daily reviews cuts the swing ratio from 9.5× to 1.8×; shorter delivery waits and a simpler network take it to 1.2×. Diamonds use safety stock tuned toward a training-period fill target, without guaranteeing equal subsequent availability.](charts/e08_structure.png){#fig-structure fig-alt="Daily replenishment accounts for the largest reduction along the modeled structural changes."}

Daily ordering alone initially lowers fulfillment by 1.45 percentage points; shorter delivery delays restore it. Across the complete structural change, median on-hand stock falls from 48.3 to 6.9 days and fulfillment rises from 97.4% to 98.4%.

The filter explains why the change is substantial. With the modeled parameters, the traditional cascade reaches variance gain 17.2× at a two-week cycle. The quick-commerce filter remains below 1.8× at every frequency (@fig-gain).

![**Shorter, daily cycles sharply reduce amplification.** Curves show frequency-specific variance gains under the unconstrained policy with fixed safety stock. The shared-sales curve assumes aligned review windows; the traditional simulation instead uses staggered review dates. At a 52-week cycle, traditional gain is still 1.58×: unit gain is the limit as cycle length tends to infinity.](charts/theory_gain.png){#fig-gain fig-alt="Traditional theoretical gain reaches about seventeen at short cycles, while quick-commerce gain stays below two."}

Shared sales replace the cascade with the sum in @prp-tiers. In this aligned-clock calculation, sharing strongly damps cycles shorter than about 30 weeks but slightly increases gain at longer cycles. Information sharing is therefore not a reduction at every frequency.

Its overall effect in the full simulation is nevertheless large for traditional retail: forecasting from store sales cuts amplification by 71.4%, with little change in fulfillment. The quick-commerce reduction is only 2.1% (@fig-shared-sales), because its incoming daily orders already contain much less distortion.

![**Sharing store sales matters where orders hide demand.** Rows show what the upstream tiers forecast from. In traditional retail, forecasting from store sales instead of incoming orders cuts the swing ratio from 9.0× to 2.6×. Quick-commerce orders already track shopper input more closely, so changing the forecast signal adds little. Hollow circles repeat each case under a recurring supply shortage. Note the different horizontal scales.](charts/e09_shared_sales.png){#fig-shared-sales fig-alt="Shared store sales substantially reduce traditional amplification and make a small difference in quick commerce."}

Slow movements can also conceal amplification of faster fluctuations.

::: {#cor-slow}
## Slow variation can dilute the measured bullwhip

Let $X=X_s+X_f$, with components uncorrelated at every lag. If their filtered variance ratios satisfy $\mathcal B_s<\mathcal B_f$, then
$$
\mathcal B=w\mathcal B_s+(1-w)\mathcal B_f,\qquad
w=\frac{\operatorname{Var}X_s}{\operatorname{Var}X}.
$$
Removing the slow component raises the ratio. For variation concentrated sufficiently near zero frequency, $\mathcal B_s$ approaches one.
:::

::: {.proof}
The input and filtered-output variances each add across the two uncorrelated components. Dividing their sums gives the weighted average.
:::

Consistent with this mechanism, the traditional simulation’s ratio rises from 9.0× raw to 24.7× after detrending. This is evidence about the chosen trend removal, not a claim that every seasonal adjustment must increase the ratio.

The channel ranking holds across forecast settings—traditional 2.4×–30.2× versus quick commerce 1.07×–1.36×—after detrending, and for both fast and intermittent sellers.

## Fragmentation shifts the problem to inventory

Dividing an unchanged catchment among more stores leaves each location needing its own buffer.

::: {#prp-fragmentation}
## Safety allowances under fragmentation

Let integer protection-horizon demand $D$ have mean $\mu>0$ and variance $\sigma^2>0$. Independently allocate each unit among $k$ stores with equal probabilities. With a common safety factor $z>0$, the sum of their allowances $z\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}D_j}$ increases relative to the unsplit allowance by
$$
r_k=\sqrt{1+\frac{k-1}{\Phi}},\qquad \Phi=\frac{\sigma^2}{\mu}.
$$
:::

The proof is in the appendix. The proportional penalty is larger at lower dispersion $\Phi$, not necessarily at lower sales volume. In this sample, intermittent products have lower dispersion over the dark stores' two-day protection horizon (median $\Phi$ 2.68 against 4.37 for fast sellers). Summed over each product's ten catchments, the formula predicts that twenty-way splitting multiplies safety allowances by 2.71 for intermittent products and 2.15 for fast sellers.

This result concerns leaf safety allowances, rather than all inventory across the network. The simulation shows the same ordering across segments: splitting each catchment twenty ways raises whole-network on-hand stock by a factor of 3.33 for intermittent products and 1.76 for fast sellers.

Overall, median stock rises from 6.9 to 13.8 days, fulfillment falls from 98.4% to 91.9%, and orders become calmer (@fig-fragmentation). More inventory and lower order variance can coexist with worse availability.

![**More dark stores mean more stock, yet calmer orders.** The same shoppers are split across 1 to 20 dark stores per original store. Stock held across the network rises steeply, most of all for slow, patchy sellers, while order swings at the brand fall. Fulfillment deteriorates alongside calmer orders: the share of demand served drops from 98.4% to 91.9%.](charts/e13_fragmentation.png){#fig-fragmentation fig-alt="Fragmentation increases inventory, especially for intermittent products, while availability deteriorates."}

## Openings and migration change the stock balance

Orders arriving at a brand finance both shopper purchases and changes in inventory.

::: {#prp-accounting}
## Orders, inventory and lost sales

Suppose brand orders are dispatched immediately, with no spoilage, returns or other external inventory flows. Over a window $W$, let $I$ include all on-hand and in-transit stock. Then
$$
\sum_W O^{\mathrm{brand}}-\sum_W D
=\Delta I_W-\mathrm{Lost}_W.
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
Internal shipments only move stock within the system. Brand dispatches add stock and completed sales remove it, so $\Delta I_W=\sum_W O^{\mathrm{brand}}-\sum_W\mathrm{sales}$. Substitute $\mathrm{sales}=D-\mathrm{Lost}$.
:::

The identity separates cumulative inventory movements from demand changes. Their timing depends on replenishment decisions.

If store openings are synchronized, opening purchases can arrive together. The expansion scenario produces a peak weekly orders-to-input ratio of 1.37×; staggering openings reduces it to 1.07× (@fig-expansion). After expansion settles, the swing ratio is 1.16×, with no detectable increase over an established network of the same size.

![**Opening stores together sends brief spikes to the brand.** Brand orders (blue) and shopper input (black), relative to the weekly level before openings, while each catchment grows from 1 to 10 dark stores (bottom panel). Shopper input is held fixed across scenarios, but synchronized openings add short spikes in brand orders. Staggering the openings across catchments removes most of them (not shown).](charts/e14_expansion.png){#fig-expansion fig-alt="Synchronized store openings briefly separate brand orders from unchanged shopper input."}

A channel switch reverses the inventory movement. In the scenario where quick commerce’s share rises from 10% to 70% over 26 weeks, traditional destocking exceeds quick-commerce stockbuilding (@fig-migration).

![**When shoppers switch channels, the brand sees a dip, not a surge.** Quick commerce's share rises from 10% to 70% over 26 weeks (bottom panel). Traditional orders fall faster than quick-commerce orders rise, as distributors run down their stock. Combined brand orders (gold) therefore run below shopper input (black) through the switch, by about four weeks of purchases in total.](charts/e15_migration.png){#fig-migration fig-alt="Traditional destocking outweighs quick-commerce inventory building during the channel switch."}

In days of total pre-switch average input, @prp-accounting gives the rounded decomposition
$$
\underbrace{-27.6}_{\text{orders minus input}}
=
\underbrace{-25.0}_{\text{physical stock change}}
-
\underbrace{2.6}_{\text{unmet demand}}.
$$
This is a gap against shopper input, not completed sales or a no-switch control. Afterward, the swing ratio is 2.52× against 2.57× in an established 70%-quick-commerce network. A brand could mistake the temporary destocking gap for falling shopper demand.

## Implications for brand teams

- **Prioritize replenishment cadence and delivery time.** Daily reviews produce the largest structural reduction, while shorter waits protect availability.
- **Share sell-through with traditional partners.** The 71.4% reduction shows the value of replacing distorted orders with sales information.
- **Monitor stock and availability beside order variance.** Fragmentation doubles stock while lowering fulfillment; calm orders alone are insufficient.
- **Account separately for openings and channel migration.** Stagger opening fills where possible and distinguish distributor destocking from demand decline.

## Scope

This is a simulation driven by real Walmart US sales, with channel structures modeled rather than measured on Indian platforms. Recorded sales already conceal historical stockouts. The theorems describe an unconstrained policy; the simulator adds nonnegative orders, lost shelf sales and safety-stock revisions. These changes need not move variance in a universal direction. Shared-data theory assumes aligned review windows, whereas the traditional simulation staggers reviews. The findings concern the modeled operating arrangements, not a universal ownership structure or a forecast of platform growth.

## Appendix: the math

Faster fluctuations induce larger target adjustments in the linear policy.

::: {#lem-gain}
## Shape of the gain

Under @thm-filter, $|H(e^{-i\omega})|^2$ increases with $\omega$ on $[0,\pi]$, from one to
$$
\left(1+\frac{2ma}{2-a}\right)^2.
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
Set $c=\cos\omega$, $u=1+ma$ and $v=\beta+ma$. Then
$$
|H|^2=\frac{N(c)}{D(c)}
=\frac{u^2+v^2-2uvc}{1+\beta^2-2\beta c}.
$$
Its derivative with respect to $c$ has numerator
$$
N'D-ND'=2(\beta u-v)(u-\beta v).
$$
Here $\beta u-v=-ma^2<0$, while
$$
u-\beta v=(1-\beta^2)+ma(1-\beta)>0.
$$
Thus gain decreases with $c$ and increases with $\omega$. Substituting $\omega=0,\pi$ gives the endpoints.
:::

Independent period demand gives a compact benchmark.

::: {#cor-iid}
## Independent-demand benchmark

For i.i.d. review-period demand,
$$
\mathcal B=1+2ma+\frac{2m^2a^2}{2-a}.
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
Stationary smoothing gives $\operatorname{Var}F=a\sigma^2/(2-a)$. Since $X_t$ and $F_{t-1}$ are independent, apply variance addition to $q_t=(1+ma)X_t-maF_{t-1}$.
:::

This is the exponential-smoothing structure analyzed by Chen, Ryan and Simchi-Levi (2000), using our protection-horizon convention.

Weekly summation of a stationary daily input/output pair reweights the spectrum by the squared gain of the seven-day sum filter. Weekly-reviewed pulse orders instead require review-period analysis; they are not a stationary daily filter output.

Splitting units adds uncertainty about where demand appears, even when total demand is unchanged.

::: {.proof}
For @prp-fragmentation,
$$
D_j\mid D\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(D,1/k).
$$
Total variance gives
$$
\operatorname{Var}D_j
=\operatorname{Var}(D/k)+E[D(1/k)(1-1/k)]
=\frac{\sigma^2+(k-1)\mu}{k^2}.
$$
Summing $k$ equal safety allowances and dividing by $z\sigma$ yields $r_k$. For heterogeneous catchments $c$, the combined ratio is instead
$$
\frac{\sum_c\sqrt{\sigma_c^2+(k-1)\mu_c}}{\sum_c\sigma_c},
$$
which cannot generally be obtained by inserting median dispersion into $r_k$.
:::

## Method

The M5 sample contains 190 food items across ten Walmart stores in three states during 2011–2016: 100 fast sellers and 90 eligible intermittent sellers. Selection and initialization use the first year only. Simulation spans days 365–1941; measurement uses days 505–1939 after 140 settling days.

Traditional reviews are weekly with tier lead times 3/5/7 days; quick-commerce reviews are daily with lead times 1/3 days. Forecast responsiveness is $\alpha=0.05$, with safety factor 1.65. Shelf shortages lose sales, upstream obligations are backlogged, and brand supply is unlimited. Ratios use weekly sums; detrending removes a centered 13-week moving average from orders and input. Physical accounting is checked to relative tolerance $10^{-5}$. Code is available on request.
